claim: Dithranol has remained one of the most effective anti-psoriatic agents despite the introduction of biologics.
source: Despite the introduction of biologics, topical dithranol (anthralin) has remained one of the most effective anti-psoriatic agents.
evidence: This is stated directly in the abstract as a general assertion about dithranol's effectiveness.

claim: Top differentially expressed genes in the early response to dithranol belonged to keratinocyte and epidermal differentiation pathways and IL-1 family members (i.e. IL36RN).
source: Top differentially expressed genes in the early response to dithranol belonged to keratinocyte and epidermal differentiation pathways and IL-1 family members (i.e. IL36RN) but not elements of the IL-17/IL-23 axis.
evidence: This claim is supported by microarray data analysis presented in the manuscript showing differential gene expression patterns.

claim: Top differentially expressed genes in the early response to dithranol did not include elements of the IL-17/IL-23 axis.
source: Top differentially expressed genes in the early response to dithranol belonged to keratinocyte and epidermal differentiation pathways and IL-1 family members (i.e. IL36RN) but not elements of the IL-17/IL-23 axis.
evidence: This is supported by the microarray analysis showing which genes were differentially expressed.

claim: Dithranol treatment led to rapid decrease in expression of keratinocyte differentiation regulators (e.g. involucrin, SERPINB7 and SERPINB13).
source: In human psoriatic response to dithranol, rapid decrease in expression of keratinocyte differentiation regulators (e.g. involucrin, SERPINB7 and SERPINB13), antimicrobial peptides (e.g. ß-defensins like DEFB4A, DEFB4B, DEFB103A, S100 proteins like S100A7, S100A12), chemotactic factors for neutrophils (e.g. CXCL5, CXCL8) and neutrophilic infiltration was followed with much delay by reduction in T cell infiltration.
evidence: This is supported by microarray and RT-PCR data showing decreased expression of these genes.

claim: Dithranol treatment led to rapid decrease in expression of antimicrobial peptides (e.g. ß-defensins like DEFB4A, DEFB4B, DEFB103A, S100 proteins like S100A7, S100A12).
source: In human psoriatic response to dithranol, rapid decrease in expression of keratinocyte differentiation regulators (e.g. involucrin, SERPINB7 and SERPINB13), antimicrobial peptides (e.g. ß-defensins like DEFB4A, DEFB4B, DEFB103A, S100 proteins like S100A7, S100A12), chemotactic factors for neutrophils (e.g. CXCL5, CXCL8) and neutrophilic infiltration was followed with much delay by reduction in T cell infiltration.
evidence: This is supported by microarray data showing differential gene expression of these antimicrobial peptides.

claim: Dithranol treatment led to rapid decrease in expression of chemotactic factors for neutrophils (e.g. CXCL5, CXCL8).
source: In human psoriatic response to dithranol, rapid decrease in expression of keratinocyte differentiation regulators (e.g. involucrin, SERPINB7 and SERPINB13), antimicrobial peptides (e.g. ß-defensins like DEFB4A, DEFB4B, DEFB103A, S100 proteins like S100A7, S100A12), chemotactic factors for neutrophils (e.g. CXCL5, CXCL8) and neutrophilic infiltration was followed with much delay by reduction in T cell infiltration.
evidence: This is supported by microarray data showing decreased expression of these chemokines.

claim: Dithranol treatment led to rapid decrease in neutrophilic infiltration.
source: In human psoriatic response to dithranol, rapid decrease in expression of keratinocyte differentiation regulators (e.g. involucrin, SERPINB7 and SERPINB13), antimicrobial peptides (e.g. ß-defensins like DEFB4A, DEFB4B, DEFB103A, S100 proteins like S100A7, S100A12), chemotactic factors for neutrophils (e.g. CXCL5, CXCL8) and neutrophilic infiltration was followed with much delay by reduction in T cell infiltration.
evidence: This is supported by immunohistochemistry data showing decreased neutrophil counts (MPO staining) at week 2-3.

claim: Reduction in T cell infiltration occurred with much delay after dithranol treatment.
source: In human psoriatic response to dithranol, rapid decrease in expression of keratinocyte differentiation regulators (e.g. involucrin, SERPINB7 and SERPINB13), antimicrobial peptides (e.g. ß-defensins like DEFB4A, DEFB4B, DEFB103A, S100 proteins like S100A7, S100A12), chemotactic factors for neutrophils (e.g. CXCL5, CXCL8) and neutrophilic infiltration was followed with much delay by reduction in T cell infiltration.
evidence: This is supported by immunohistochemistry data showing T cell counts were only significantly reduced at follow-up (4-6 weeks after end of treatment).

claim: Targeting keratinocytes rather than immune cells may be an alternative approach for topical anti-psoriatic treatment.
source: Targeting keratinocytes rather than immune cells may be an alternative approach in particular for topical anti-psoriatic treatment, an area with high need for new drugs.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the study's findings about dithranol's mechanism of action.

claim: There is high need for new drugs in topical anti-psoriatic treatment.
source: Targeting keratinocytes rather than immune cells may be an alternative approach in particular for topical anti-psoriatic treatment, an area with high need for new drugs.
evidence: This is stated as background knowledge about the current state of psoriasis treatment.

claim: Biologics targeting IL-17 or IL-23 exhibit high efficacy in psoriasis treatment.
source: Currently, targeted therapy with antibodies against IL-17 or IL-23 exhibits high efficacy and allows complete or almost complete clinical clearance of psoriasis lesions in a high percentage of cases (Blauvelt et al., 2017; Langley et al., 2014; Papp et al., 2017; Reich et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published clinical studies.

claim: Biologics targeting IL-17 or IL-23 allow complete or almost complete clinical clearance of psoriasis lesions in a high percentage of cases.
source: Currently, targeted therapy with antibodies against IL-17 or IL-23 exhibits high efficacy and allows complete or almost complete clinical clearance of psoriasis lesions in a high percentage of cases (Blauvelt et al., 2017; Langley et al., 2014; Papp et al., 2017; Reich et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published clinical studies.

claim: Patients with limited body area involvement (mild forms of psoriasis) represent up to 90% of psoriasis patients.
source: However, patients with limited body area involvement (i.e. mild forms of psoriasis) who represent the majority of psoriasis patients with up to 90% (Stern et al., 2004) have been neglected.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a published study.

claim: Patients with mild forms of psoriasis have been neglected in recent treatment developments.
source: However, patients with limited body area involvement (i.e. mild forms of psoriasis) who represent the majority of psoriasis patients with up to 90% (Stern et al., 2004) have been neglected.
evidence: This is an assertion based on the observation that most innovation has focused on systemic treatments rather than topical treatments.

claim: Not much innovation has occurred in topical treatment of psoriasis in recent years.
source: Not much innovation has occurred in the past few years on topical treatment of psoriasis that is mainly prescribed to these patients.
evidence: This is stated as an observation about the field of psoriasis treatment.

claim: Steroids, vitamin D3 and vitamin A analogues are most commonly used as topical agents in psoriasis patients.
source: Steroids, vitamin D3 and vitamin A analogues are most commonly used as topical agents in such patients, but besides changes in their pharmaceutical formulation, they have not been developed further in recent years (de Korte et al., 2008; Krueger et al., 2001; Langley et al., 2011; Schaarschmidt et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published studies.

claim: Topical steroids, vitamin D3 and vitamin A analogues have not been developed further in recent years besides changes in their pharmaceutical formulation.
source: Steroids, vitamin D3 and vitamin A analogues are most commonly used as topical agents in such patients, but besides changes in their pharmaceutical formulation, they have not been developed further in recent years (de Korte et al., 2008; Krueger et al., 2001; Langley et al., 2011; Schaarschmidt et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published studies.

claim: Short courses of dithranol have been successfully used as intermittent topical treatment of psoriasis since 1916.
source: Short courses of dithranol (1,8-dihydroxy-9-anthracenone or anthralin) have been successfully used as intermittent topical treatment of psoriasis since 1916 (Nast et al., 2012; Sehgal et al., 2014; Vleuten et al., 1996).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published studies.

claim: Dithranol has disadvantages including brown staining and irritation of perilesional skin.
source: Despite its numerous disadvantages like brown staining and irritation of perilesional skin, dithranol has remained one of the most effective topical treatment modalities in psoriasis.
evidence: This is stated as known characteristics of dithranol treatment.

claim: Dithranol delivers PASI75 rates in 66–82.5% of patients.
source: Analogous to the most recent generation of biologics (including anti-IL-17 and anti-IL-23 antibodies), dithranol delivers PASI75 rates in 66–82.5% of patients with fast action and clearance of skin lesion within very few weeks (Kemény et al., 1990; Painsi et al., 2015b; Sehgal et al., 2014; van de Kerkhof, 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published studies.

claim: Dithranol achieves clearance of skin lesions within very few weeks.
source: Analogous to the most recent generation of biologics (including anti-IL-17 and anti-IL-23 antibodies), dithranol delivers PASI75 rates in 66–82.5% of patients with fast action and clearance of skin lesion within very few weeks (Kemény et al., 1990; Painsi et al., 2015b; Sehgal et al., 2014; van de Kerkhof, 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published studies.

claim: Dithranol's exact mechanism of action has remained largely unknown despite many years of use.
source: Although dithranol has been used for many years, its exact mechanism of action has remained largely unknown (Holstein et al., 2017; Kemény et al., 1990; Kucharekova et al., 2006; Sehgal et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published studies.

claim: The study employed the c-Jun/JunB knockout model to investigate dithranol's mechanism.
source: With the aim of unraveling dithranol's therapeutic mechanisms and to possibly uncover new targets for topical treatment of psoriasis, we conducted a clinical trial and employed several mouse models including the c-Jun/JunB knockout model (Zenz et al., 2005) and the imiquimod psoriasis model (van der Fits et al., 2009) in order to address this issue and elucidate dithranol's effects.
evidence: This is stated as part of the study design.

claim: The study employed the imiquimod psoriasis model to investigate dithranol's mechanism.
source: With the aim of unraveling dithranol's therapeutic mechanisms and to possibly uncover new targets for topical treatment of psoriasis, we conducted a clinical trial and employed several mouse models including the c-Jun/JunB knockout model (Zenz et al., 2005) and the imiquimod psoriasis model (van der Fits et al., 2009) in order to address this issue and elucidate dithranol's effects.
evidence: This is stated as part of the study design.

claim: Dithranol exerts its anti-psoriatic effects by directly targeting keratinocytes and their crosstalk with neutrophils.
source: In this study, we demonstrate that dithranol exerts its anti-psoriatic effects by directly targeting keratinocytes and their crosstalk with neutrophils, as well as disrupting the IL-36 inflammatory loop.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the study's experimental data including microarray analysis and immunohistochemistry.

claim: Dithranol exerts its anti-psoriatic effects by disrupting the IL-36 inflammatory loop.
source: In this study, we demonstrate that dithranol exerts its anti-psoriatic effects by directly targeting keratinocytes and their crosstalk with neutrophils, as well as disrupting the IL-36 inflammatory loop.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the study's experimental data showing decreased expression of IL-36 related genes.

claim: Dithranol's therapeutic activity was completely independent of its pro-inflammatory effect mainly on perilesional skin.
source: Consistent with this finding, we observed that dithranol's therapeutic activity was completely independent of its pro-inflammatory effect mainly on perilesional skin, thus overthrowing the long-believed paradigm that dithranol-induced irritation is crucial for its anti-psoriatic action and unraveling irritation merely as a bystander effect of treatment.
evidence: This is supported by data showing no correlation between dithranol-induced erythema and its anti-psoriatic effect.

claim: The long-believed paradigm that dithranol-induced irritation is crucial for its anti-psoriatic action is incorrect.
source: Consistent with this finding, we observed that dithranol's therapeutic activity was completely independent of its pro-inflammatory effect mainly on perilesional skin, thus overthrowing the long-believed paradigm that dithranol-induced irritation is crucial for its anti-psoriatic action and unraveling irritation merely as a bystander effect of treatment.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the study's data showing no correlation between irritation and therapeutic effect.

claim: Dithranol-induced irritation is merely a bystander effect of treatment.
source: Consistent with this finding, we observed that dithranol's therapeutic activity was completely independent of its pro-inflammatory effect mainly on perilesional skin, thus overthrowing the long-believed paradigm that dithranol-induced irritation is crucial for its anti-psoriatic action and unraveling irritation merely as a bystander effect of treatment.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the study's data showing no correlation between irritation and therapeutic effect.

claim: Dithranol led to a fast reduction of psoriatic skin lesions in most of the 15 patients of the study.
source: As depicted in Figure 1C (and Figure 1—figure supplement 1), dithranol did lead to a fast reduction of psoriatic skin lesions in most of the 15 patients of the study, as determined by psoriasis area and severity index (PASI) and local psoriasis severity index (PSI) of marker lesions.
evidence: This is supported by clinical data shown in Figure 1C and Table 1.

claim: The mean decrease in PASI score was 58% after 2–3 weeks of dithranol treatment.
source: As shown in Table 1, the mean decrease in PASI score was 58% after 2–3 weeks, confirming its high clinical efficacy (Painsi et al., 2015a; Painsi et al., 2015b; Swinkels et al., 2004).
evidence: This is supported by clinical data presented in Table 1.

claim: Dithranol treatment led to a visible inflammatory response only at perilesional skin sites, but not within psoriatic plaques.
source: Remarkably, dithranol treatment did lead to a visible inflammatory response only at perilesional skin sites, but not within psoriatic plaques and there was no correlation between dithranol-induced erythema and its anti-psoriatic effect (Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is supported by clinical observations and data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2.

claim: There was no correlation between dithranol-induced erythema and its anti-psoriatic effect.
source: Remarkably, dithranol treatment did lead to a visible inflammatory response only at perilesional skin sites, but not within psoriatic plaques and there was no correlation between dithranol-induced erythema and its anti-psoriatic effect (Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is supported by correlation analysis shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2.

claim: Dithranol application led to a significant reduction in epidermal hyperplasia.
source: Dithranol application led to a significant reduction in epidermal hyperplasia (as measured by thickness of epidermis).
evidence: This is supported by histological analysis data shown in Figure 2.

claim: There was no significant change in dermal infiltrate score during dithranol treatment.
source: Intriguingly, there was no significant change in dermal infiltrate score during treatment.
evidence: This is supported by histological analysis data shown in Figure 2.

claim: At the follow-up visit, hyperplasia of the epidermis was reduced further after dithranol treatment.
source: At the follow-up visit, hyperplasia of the epidermis was reduced further and cellular infiltrate in the dermis was significantly diminished (Figure 2).
evidence: This is supported by histological analysis data shown in Figure 2.

claim: At the follow-up visit, cellular infiltrate in the dermis was significantly diminished after dithranol treatment.
source: At the follow-up visit, hyperplasia of the epidermis was reduced further and cellular infiltrate in the dermis was significantly diminished (Figure 2).
evidence: This is supported by histological analysis data shown in Figure 2.

claim: Dithranol slowly diminished CD3, CD4, FoxP3 and CD8 cell counts in the dermis.
source: Dithranol slowly diminished CD3, CD4, FoxP3 and CD8 cell counts in the dermis as evidenced by unaffected cell numbers early on during the treatment course and significant reduction only at the follow-up visit (4–6 weeks after end of treatment) (Figure 2).
evidence: This is supported by immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 2.

claim: T cell counts in the dermis were unaffected early on during dithranol treatment.
source: Dithranol slowly diminished CD3, CD4, FoxP3 and CD8 cell counts in the dermis as evidenced by unaffected cell numbers early on during the treatment course and significant reduction only at the follow-up visit (4–6 weeks after end of treatment) (Figure 2).
evidence: This is supported by immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 2.

claim: T cell counts in the dermis showed significant reduction only at the follow-up visit (4–6 weeks after end of treatment).
source: Dithranol slowly diminished CD3, CD4, FoxP3 and CD8 cell counts in the dermis as evidenced by unaffected cell numbers early on during the treatment course and significant reduction only at the follow-up visit (4–6 weeks after end of treatment) (Figure 2).
evidence: This is supported by immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 2.

claim: The response of T cells in the epidermis to dithranol occurred earlier than in the dermis.
source: The response of T cells in the epidermis occurred a little earlier, with significant reduction present already at the end of treatment (week 2–3) (Figure 2).
evidence: This is supported by immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 2.

claim: Dithranol led to a fast decrease in epidermal hyperproliferation (epidermal thickness, Ki-67 and CK16 staining) at end of treatment (week 2–3).
source: In agreement with other studies (Holstein et al., 2017; Swinkels et al., 2002a; Vleuten et al., 1996; Yamamoto and Nishioka, 2003), we found a fast decrease in epidermal hyperproliferation (epidermal thickness, Ki-67 and CK16 staining) at end of treatment (week 2–3).
evidence: This is supported by histological and immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 2, and is consistent with previous studies.

claim: Neutrophil numbers in epidermis and dermis were significantly reduced at end of treatment (week 2–3) with dithranol.
source: Neutrophil numbers (as assessed by myeloperoxidase staining) in epidermis and dermis were also significantly reduced at that time point.
evidence: This is supported by immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 2.

claim: An increase in the number of Langerhans cells in the epidermis was detected at the follow-up visit after dithranol treatment.
source: An increase in the number of Langerhans cells in the epidermis (as indicated by CD1a staining) was detected at the follow-up visit.
evidence: This is supported by immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 2.

claim: Dithranol led to differential expression of 62 genes at day 6 of treatment compared to baseline, including 17 genes with reduced and 45 genes with increased expression.
source: Microarray analysis comparing lesional skin at day 6 of treatment with lesional skin samples at baseline revealed that dithranol led to differential expression of 62 genes including 17 genes with reduced and 45 genes with increased expression.
evidence: This is supported by microarray data analysis.

claim: Dithranol upregulated genes involved in keratinization and keratinocyte differentiation (e.g. KRT2, LCE1C, KRT73, LCE1A) at day 6.
source: Among these differentially expressed genes (DEGs), there was a significant upregulation of genes involved in keratinization and keratinocyte differentiation (e.g. KRT2, LCE1C, KRT73, LCE1A) and establishment of skin barrier (e.g. FLG2, HRNR, FLG).
evidence: This is supported by microarray data shown in Table 2.

claim: Dithranol upregulated genes involved in establishment of skin barrier (e.g. FLG2, HRNR, FLG) at day 6.
source: Among these differentially expressed genes (DEGs), there was a significant upregulation of genes involved in keratinization and keratinocyte differentiation (e.g. KRT2, LCE1C, KRT73, LCE1A) and establishment of skin barrier (e.g. FLG2, HRNR, FLG).
evidence: This is supported by microarray data shown in Table 2.

claim: Dithranol downregulated genes of antimicrobial peptides such as ß-defensin-2 (DEFB4A, DEFB4B) at day 6.
source: Furthermore, dithranol downregulated genes of antimicrobial peptides (AMPs) such as ß-defensin-2 (DEFB4A, DEFB4B) and chemoattractants for neutrophils (e.g. CXCL5, CXCL8, PPBP1, TREM1) (Table 2).
evidence: This is supported by microarray data shown in Table 2.

claim: Dithranol downregulated chemoattractants for neutrophils (e.g. CXCL5, CXCL8, PPBP1, TREM1) at day 6.
source: Furthermore, dithranol downregulated genes of antimicrobial peptides (AMPs) such as ß-defensin-2 (DEFB4A, DEFB4B) and chemoattractants for neutrophils (e.g. CXCL5, CXCL8, PPBP1, TREM1) (Table 2).
evidence: This is supported by microarray data shown in Table 2.

claim: At the end of treatment (week 2–3), dithranol had deregulated a total of 453 genes, with downregulation of 325 DEGs and upregulation of 128 genes.
source: At the end of treatment (week 2–3), dithranol had deregulated a total of 453 genes, with downregulation of 325 DEGs and upregulation of 128 genes.
evidence: This is supported by microarray data analysis.

claim: Expression of various genes involved in keratinocyte differentiation decreased further upon dithranol treatment at week 2-3 compared to day 6.
source: Compared to day 6, expression of various genes involved in keratinocyte differentiation decreased further upon dithranol treatment and other AMPs (e.g. S100A7A, S100A12, DEFB103A) and genes involved in neutrophil-mediated inflammatory responses significantly diminished in their expression.
evidence: This is supported by microarray data analysis comparing different time points.

claim: Other AMPs (e.g. S100A7A, S100A12, DEFB103A) significantly diminished in their expression at week 2-3.
source: Compared to day 6, expression of various genes involved in keratinocyte differentiation decreased further upon dithranol treatment and other AMPs (e.g. S100A7A, S100A12, DEFB103A) and genes involved in neutrophil-mediated inflammatory responses significantly diminished in their expression.
evidence: This is supported by microarray data shown in Table 3.

claim: Genes involved in neutrophil-mediated inflammatory responses significantly diminished in their expression at week 2-3.
source: Compared to day 6, expression of various genes involved in keratinocyte differentiation decreased further upon dithranol treatment and other AMPs (e.g. S100A7A, S100A12, DEFB103A) and genes involved in neutrophil-mediated inflammatory responses significantly diminished in their expression.
evidence: This is supported by microarray data analysis.

claim: Dithranol lowered expression of inflammatory response-related genes (e.g. IL1B, IL17, IL22, IL36A, IL36G, IL36RN) only at the end of treatment (week 2–3) with delay.
source: With delay, dithranol also lowered expression of inflammatory response-related genes (e.g. IL1B, IL17, IL22, IL36A, IL36G, IL36RN) only at the end of treatment (week 2–3) (Table 3).
evidence: This is supported by microarray data shown in Table 3.

claim: Genes involved in T-cell activation were not differentially expressed during dithranol treatment up to week 2–3.
source: Notably, genes involved in T-cell activation were not differentially expressed in the observation period (during dithranol up to week 2–3).
evidence: This is supported by microarray data analysis.

claim: Ratios of microarray target genes strongly correlated with those obtained from Nanostring analysis at day 6 (r = 0.8830).
source: To verify a subset of differentially expressed genes from the microarray data, we performed nCounter Nanostring analysis on 80 target and four reference genes. Ratios of microarray target genes strongly correlated with those obtained from Nanostring analysis at the early (day 6) (r = 0.8830) and late time point examined at the end of dithranol treatment (week 2–3) (r = 0.8859) (Supplementary file 2).
evidence: This is supported by correlation analysis between microarray and Nanostring data.

claim: Ratios of microarray target genes strongly correlated with those obtained from Nanostring analysis at week 2–3 (r = 0.8859).
source: To verify a subset of differentially expressed genes from the microarray data, we performed nCounter Nanostring analysis on 80 target and four reference genes. Ratios of microarray target genes strongly correlated with those obtained from Nanostring analysis at the early (day 6) (r = 0.8830) and late time point examined at the end of dithranol treatment (week 2–3) (r = 0.8859) (Supplementary file 2).
evidence: This is supported by correlation analysis between microarray and Nanostring data.

claim: GO terms related to keratinization (e.g. keratinocyte differentiation, establishment of skin barrier) were among the most significant GO groups at day 6 vs. baseline.
source: Comparing day 6 vs. baseline, we found gene ontology (GO) terms related to keratinization (e.g. keratinocyte differentiation, establishment of skin barrier) and neutrophil chemotaxis (e.g. neutrophil migration, regulation of neutrophil migration) among the most significant GO groups (Table 4).
evidence: This is supported by gene ontology enrichment analysis shown in Table 4.

claim: GO terms related to neutrophil chemotaxis (e.g. neutrophil migration, regulation of neutrophil migration) were among the most significant GO groups at day 6 vs. baseline.
source: Comparing day 6 vs. baseline, we found gene ontology (GO) terms related to keratinization (e.g. keratinocyte differentiation, establishment of skin barrier) and neutrophil chemotaxis (e.g. neutrophil migration, regulation of neutrophil migration) among the most significant GO groups (Table 4).
evidence: This is supported by gene ontology enrichment analysis shown in Table 4.

claim: Top significantly enriched GO terms at week 2–3 vs. baseline were related to immune response (e.g. inflammatory response, cytokine secretion).
source: Top significantly enriched GO terms at week 2–3 vs. baseline were related to immune response (e.g. inflammatory response, cytokine secretion) and differentiation of keratinocytes (e.g. epidermis development, keratinization) (Table 5).
evidence: This is supported by gene ontology enrichment analysis shown in Table 5.

claim: Top significantly enriched GO terms at week 2–3 vs. baseline were related to differentiation of keratinocytes (e.g. epidermis development, keratinization).
source: Top significantly enriched GO terms at week 2–3 vs. baseline were related to immune response (e.g. inflammatory response, cytokine secretion) and differentiation of keratinocytes (e.g. epidermis development, keratinization) (Table 5).
evidence: This is supported by gene ontology enrichment analysis shown in Table 5.

claim: At follow-up (4–6 weeks after end of treatment), 10 of 13 patients showed >50% reduction in epidermal thickness and >75% reduction in Ki67 staining.
source: At follow-up (4–6 weeks after end of treatment), 10 of 13 patients showed >50% reduction in epidermal thickness and >75% reduction in Ki67 staining.
evidence: This is supported by histological analysis data.

claim: 10 patients with >50% reduction in epidermal thickness and >75% reduction in Ki67 staining were classified as histological responders.
source: These 10 patients were classified as histological responders.
evidence: This is stated as the classification criteria used in the study.

claim: 131 genes were differentially expressed in histological responders compared to non-responders at end of treatment (week 2–3).
source: Microarray gene expression analysis at end of treatment (week 2–3) revealed that 131 genes were differentially expressed in histological responders compared to non-responders, predicting histological outcome for the follow-up time point 4–6 weeks after the end of treatment.
evidence: This is supported by microarray data analysis.

claim: Pathways like keratinocyte differentiation, cornification and keratin filament formation were among the top 20 GO terms for genes differentially expressed in histological responders compared to non-responders.
source: Using gene ontology enrichment analysis of these DEGs, we found pathways like keratinocyte differentiation, cornification and keratin filament formation among the top 20 GO terms (Supplementary file 3).
evidence: This is supported by gene ontology enrichment analysis.

claim: Topical dithranol application strongly reduced psoriatic lesions in c-Jun/JunB knockout mice as measured by macroscopic overall ear thickness.
source: Topical dithranol application strongly reduced psoriatic lesions as measured by macroscopic overall ear thickness and microscopic epidermal thickness in this genetic model of psoriasis based on inducible epidermal deletion of the AP1 transcription factors c-Jun/JunB (Glitzner et al., 2014; Zenz et al., 2005; Figure 3B–D).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3.

claim: Topical dithranol application strongly reduced psoriatic lesions in c-Jun/JunB knockout mice as measured by microscopic epidermal thickness.
source: Topical dithranol application strongly reduced psoriatic lesions as measured by macroscopic overall ear thickness and microscopic epidermal thickness in this genetic model of psoriasis based on inducible epidermal deletion of the AP1 transcription factors c-Jun/JunB (Glitzner et al., 2014; Zenz et al., 2005; Figure 3B–D).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3.

claim: There was no difference in the outcome to dithranol with regard to different concentrations series in c-Jun/JunB knockout mice.
source: There was no difference in the outcome to dithranol with regard to different concentrations series, therefore, data was pooled for certain analyses as indicated (Figure 3).
evidence: This is stated as an observation from the experimental data.

claim: Dithranol downregulated genes belonging to the group of late cornified envelope genes (Lce6a, Lce1i, Lce1g, Lce1f) in c-Jun/JunB knockout mice.
source: Gene expression profiling using Clariom S mouse microarray showed that among the top 45 differentially regulated genes, dithranol downregulated genes belonging to the group of late cornified envelope genes (Lce6a, Lce1i, Lce1g, Lce1f), as well as hornerin (Hrnr) (Table 6).
evidence: This is supported by microarray data shown in Table 6.

claim: Dithranol downregulated hornerin (Hrnr) in c-Jun/JunB knockout mice.
source: Gene expression profiling using Clariom S mouse microarray showed that among the top 45 differentially regulated genes, dithranol downregulated genes belonging to the group of late cornified envelope genes (Lce6a, Lce1i, Lce1g, Lce1f), as well as hornerin (Hrnr) (Table 6).
evidence: This is supported by microarray data shown in Table 6.

claim: Skin development, epidermis development, epithelial cell differentiation and keratinization were among the top 20 significantly enriched pathways in dithranol-treated c-Jun/JunB knockout mice.
source: Gene ontology enrichment analysis of all differentially expressed genes (fold change >1.5 and p-value<0.05) revealed skin development, epidermis development, epithelial cell differentiation and keratinization among the top 20 significantly enriched pathways (Table 7).
evidence: This is supported by gene ontology enrichment analysis shown in Table 7.

claim: Associated genes found in enriched pathways in dithranol-treated c-Jun/JunB knockout mice included Flg2, Ivl, Hrnr, Lor, Krt2, Casp14, Lce1c, Serpinb7 and Serpbinb13.
source: Associated genes found were for example Flg2, Ivl, Hrnr, Lor, Krt2, Casp14, Lce1c, Serpinb7 and Serpbinb13, among others.
evidence: This is supported by gene ontology enrichment analysis.

claim: The microarray assay allowed comparison of 300 DEGs in dithranol-treated psoriasis patients (week 2–3 vs. day 0) with 336 murine DEGs from dithranol-treated c-Jun/JunB knockout mice.
source: In total, the microarray assay allowed us to compare 300 DEGs in dithranol-treated psoriasis patients (week 2–3 vs. day 0) and 18 DEGs from day 6 vs. day 0 with 336 murine DEGs from dithranol-treated c-Jun/JunB knockout mice.
evidence: This is stated as the methodology for comparing human and mouse data.

claim: Comparing DEGs from day 6 vs. day 0 with murine DEGs, there was an overlap of 11 genes.
source: Notably, comparing DEGs from day 6 vs. day 0 with murine DEGs, we found an overlap of 11 genes.
